Chapter One. Meeting Each Moment with Fresh Eyes.
You know, there’s something kind of magical about how a child sees the world. Every little thing—a sound, a color, the way sunlight hits the floor—feels brand new. It’s all possibility and wonder. And sure, as we get older, that sense of openness usually fades away. Routines settle in, we think we know how things work, and pretty soon, the world can start to feel a little... predictable.
But here’s the beautiful twist at the heart of Zen practice: it’s not about forgetting what you’ve learned. Instead, it’s about letting go of the urge to judge, to compare, or to expect. You’re invited to meet each moment as if it’s the very first time you’ve ever experienced it.
Picture someone sitting quietly in a small, sunlit room. Their legs are folded, hands resting gently in their lap. Outside, life is buzzing along, but inside, there’s this gentle hush. They’re not chasing thoughts or trying to force any particular feeling. They’re just here—just noticing the breath coming and going, the soft sounds in the air, the way light shifts across the room. There’s no pressure to prove anything, no need to hit some special state of mind. It’s just pure, open curiosity, free from the weight of what’s happened before or what might come next.
Most folks, when they first sit down to meditate, show up with a suitcase full of expectations. Maybe they’re hoping to feel calm, searching for a spark of insight, or just wanting a break from all the noise. But the funny thing is, the more tightly you hold onto those hopes, the further away peace seems to drift. Trying to force it is like chasing after a feather—the harder you reach, the more it slips away. The real shift happens when you’re willing to let go, and simply allow each breath, each thought, each sensation, to come and go on its own.
And here’s the thing—it doesn’t stop with meditation. This way of meeting the moment spills right into everyday life. Think about doing something you’ve done a thousand times—washing dishes, walking to work, or listening to a friend’s story. When your mind’s crowded with assumptions—“I know how this goes,” or “I’ve already heard this”—life gets small. But when you pause, when you soften your grip on certainty, even the most ordinary moments can feel alive and a little bit surprising.
There’s a story about someone who spent years trying to master meditation and finally asked their teacher for advice. The teacher just smiled and said, “Just sit.” No complicated instructions. No secret tricks. Just be present, let go of striving, and trust that simple act. At first, it sounded almost disappointingly easy. But over time, it became clear: the real challenge isn’t doing more—it’s learning to do less. Letting go of that need to control or perfect every experience.
That’s the heart of beginner’s mind—a gentle, open attitude that welcomes whatever shows up, without clinging or pushing away. It’s not about pretending you don’t know anything. It’s about holding your knowledge lightly, staying open to surprise, and realizing that every single moment really is, in some way, brand new.
So, life becomes less about piling up answers, and more about living the questions—one breath at a time.
